entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Cabinet of Brazil (Conselho de Ministros), the executive body comprising the President of Brazil and the ministers heading federal ministries, operates within Brazil's presidential system established by the 1988 Federal Constitution — a democratic constitution adopted after 21 years of military dictatorship (1964-1985) and designed with specific provisions to prevent executive overreach while enabling effective governance of the world's fifth-largest country.

Brazil's cabinet functions within a complex presidential-legislative relationship: the President appoints ministers and sets policy, but in Brazil's highly fragmented multi-party system (with 25+ parties typically represented in the legislature), governing requires building extensive congressional coalitions. This dynamic has produced what scholars call 'coalitional presidentialism' — the President typically distributes ministerial positions as bargaining chips to secure legislative support from coalition parties, making Brazil's cabinet a coalition-management mechanism as much as a governance tool.

The cabinet has reflected Brazil's major political transitions: the return of civilian government under José Sarney (1985), the economic stabilization under Fernando Henrique Cardoso's Plano Real (1994), the Workers' Party governments of Lula and Dilma (2003-2016), the traumatic Dilma Rousseff impeachment (2016), and Bolsonaro's military-heavy administration (2019-2022). Lula's third-term cabinet (2023-) reflects the complex of parties needed to govern in Brazil's fragmented legislature, with ministers drawn from across the political spectrum from Workers' Party to center-right parties.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Brazil's cabinet — the executive instrument of the world's fifth-largest country, operating within a distinctive coalitional presidentialism model, and reflecting the full arc from military dictatorship redemocratization to Workers' Party social programs to political crisis — is central to understanding Latin America's largest democracy.
